indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B2.4.1.2: Show understanding of the concept of heat in terms of its importance, effects, sources and transfer from one medium to another
indicator.objective: Understand that objects become hot or cold through the loss or gain of heat

skills.description: Understand that objects become hot by gaining heat and cold by losing heat
Describe what happens when things gain or lose heat

misconceptions: Cold is a kind of energy that enters an object.
Objects become cold by gaining coldness, not by losing heat.
A fridge adds cold to food.
If something is not on fire, it has no heat.
Ice is cold because it contains cold energy.

questions.stem: How does an object become hot?
hints: Think about putting a pot on a fire.
The fire gives heat to the pot.
questions.explanation: An object becomes hot when it gains heat from a heat source.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think objects become hot on their own.

questions.stem: How does an object become cold?
hints: Think about putting water in a fridge.
questions.explanation: An object becomes cold when it loses heat. The fridge removes heat from the water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think objects become cold by gaining 'coldness'.

questions.stem: Which of these is a source of heat?
questions.explanation: A lighted stove is a source of heat used for cooking.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a fan produces heat.

questions.stem: What happens to ice when you leave it in the sun?
questions.explanation: The sun gives heat to the ice, causing it to melt into water.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think ice stays solid in the sun.

questions.stem: What is the main natural source of heat on Earth?
hints: It comes out in the day.
questions.explanation: The sun is the main natural source of heat.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the moon gives off heat.

questions.stem: Why does a spoon left in a hot cup of tea feel hot after a while?
options: The spoon makes its own heat
The heat moves from the tea to the spoon
hints: Heat moves to the cooler object.
questions.explanation: Heat transfers from the hot tea to the metal spoon, making the spoon feel hot.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the spoon generates its own heat.

questions.stem: What happens to a hot iron when you unplug it and leave it for a while?
hints: It is no longer getting electricity.
It loses heat to the air.
questions.explanation: When unplugged, the iron stops gaining heat and starts losing heat to the cooler air, so it cools down.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the iron stays hot forever.

questions.stem: Kofi wants to dry his wet clothes. What source of heat can he use?
questions.explanation: The sun provides heat that helps evaporate the water from the clothes, drying them.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a fan dries clothes by adding heat.

questions.stem: When you put a bottle of water in the fridge, what happens to the heat in the water?
options: The water loses heat to the fridge
questions.explanation: The water loses heat to the cold fridge, which is why the water becomes cold.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the fridge adds 'coldness' to the water.

questions.stem: Name one thing you use in your home to make heat.
hints: You use it to iron clothes.
questions.explanation: A stove, electric iron, or heater are sources of heat in the home.

questions.stem: What happens to water when you put it in a freezer?
questions.explanation: Water loses heat in the freezer and turns into solid ice.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the freezer adds cold to the water.

questions.stem: Ama holds a cold stone in her hands. Her hands feel cold. Why?
options: The stone gives cold to her hands
The stone takes heat from her hands
The stone makes her hands wet
hints: Heat moves from hot to cold.
Her hands are warmer than the stone.
questions.explanation: The stone is colder than her hands. Heat moves from her hands to the stone, making her hands feel cold.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think cold transfers from the stone to the hands.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a source of heat?
hints: You use it to cool drinks.
questions.explanation: A block of ice is cold, not a source of heat.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all solids are hot.

questions.stem: Why does a pot of water boil when you place it on a hot stove?
options: The water gains heat from the stove
The water loses heat to the stove
The water creates its own heat
The stove cools down the water
questions.explanation: The water gains heat from the hot stove, which makes it boil.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the water gains cold from the stove.

questions.stem: Ama says 'The fridge makes my food cold by adding cold to it.' Is she right?
options: No, the fridge removes heat from the food
No, the fridge adds hot air
hints: Does cold exist on its own?
The fridge takes heat away from the food.
questions.explanation: Ama is not right. A fridge does not add 'cold'; it removes heat from the food inside, which makes the food cold.
questions.misconception: Pupils often think cold is a substance that can be added.

questions.stem: Which two sources of heat are commonly used in a Ghanaian home for cooking?
options: A charcoal stove and a gas cooker
questions.explanation: A charcoal stove and a gas cooker are common sources of heat for cooking.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name electrical items that do not produce heat.

questions.stem: Explain why a metal spoon feels hot when placed in a cup of hot tea.

criteria.description: States that heat moves from the tea to the spoon
States that the spoon gains heat and becomes hot

hints: Does heat stay in the tea or move?
questions.explanation: The spoon feels hot because it gains heat from the hot tea.

questions.stem: Explain why an ice cube melts when you hold it in your hand.

criteria.description: States that the hand is warmer than the ice
States that heat moves from the hand to the ice, causing it to melt

questions.explanation: Your hand is warmer than the ice. Heat moves from your hand to the ice, causing it to gain heat and melt.

questions.stem: A student puts a cold metal spoon in a cup of hot tea. After a while, the tea becomes slightly cooler and the spoon becomes warmer. Why?
options: The spoon added cold to the tea
Heat moved from the tea to the spoon until they reached a similar temperature
The tea lost heat to the air only
The spoon gained cold from the tea
hints: Heat moves from hot to cold.
The tea is hot, the spoon is cold.
questions.explanation: Heat moves from the hot tea to the cold spoon. The tea loses heat (so it cools slightly) and the spoon gains heat (so it warms up).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think cold transfers from the spoon to the tea.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher what happens to an object when it gains heat and what happens when it loses heat.

criteria.description: States it becomes hot when it gains heat
States it becomes cold when it loses heat

hints: Think about a pot on a fire.
Think about water in a fridge.
questions.explanation: An object becomes hot when it gains heat and cold when it loses heat.
